skill.example: 1 + i is a root of z³ − 4z² + 6z − 4 → 1 ± i, 2
needs: Solve a quadratic with complex roots
Divide a polynomial by a linear or quadratic

note: Use the SAME method as the references (they are the lesson so far); change one thing, as usual. The method: Uses the conjugate root theorem to write the quadratic factor from the pair, divides it into the polynomial and reads off the remaining root. Earlier backups were dropped for doing this instead: Finds unknown coefficients p and q using sum and product of roots rather than forming and dividing by a quadratic factor to find all roots.

lines.text: The coefficients are real, so complex roots come in conjugate pairs.

skill.title: Sketch/match the graph of f′ from f
skill.example: turning points of f ↔ roots of f′
needs: Find where a function is increasing/decreasing for all x or on intervals

note: Use the SAME method as the references (they are the lesson so far); change one thing, as usual. The method: Reads gradients at key points of f (turning points give roots of f') and plots them to sketch f'. Earlier backups were dropped for doing this instead: Differentiates and finds the minimum of f' by calculus, rather than reading f's graph to get the key points of f'.

steps.title: Read the gradient of p(x) at key points

lines.text: The value of $p'(x)$ is the gradient of $p(x)$.
At $x = 1$ and $x = 3$, $p(x)$ has a turning point, so the gradient is $0$: $p'(1) = 0$ and $p'(3) = 0$.
$p(x)$ is steepest uphill at its inflection point $x = 2$, where the gradient is at its maximum, so $p'(2) = 1$.

steps.title: Use the shape of p'(x) to find the last point

lines.text: $p(x)$ is a cubic, so $p'(x)$ is a quadratic: a U-shape upside down, with its peak at $(2, 1)$.
A quadratic is symmetric about its peak, so $x = 4$ matches $x = 0$: $p'(4) = -3$.

steps.title: Plot the points and join them

lines.text: Plot $(0, -3)$, $(1, 0)$, $(2, 1)$, $(3, 0)$ and $(4, -3)$, then draw a smooth curve through them.

steps.title: Turning points of $f$ give the roots of $f'$

lines.text: At a turning point the slope of $f$ is $0$, so $f'(-1) = 0$ and $f'(3) = 0$.
The graph of $f'$ crosses the $x$-axis at $(-1, 0)$ and $(3, 0)$.
The graph of $f'$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(0, -9)$.
